profiles.meeting_scenario: At a tertiary trauma hospital, a consultant orthopaedic trauma surgeon and the hospital's 3D imaging lead meet to plan preoperative 3D modelling support for a 29-year-old patient with a complex acetabular fracture scheduled for fixation later in the week. The immediate agenda is to agree what 3D planning materials will be produced, who will handle imaging preparation and clinical review, and when the outputs need to be available for the fracture conference and surgery. The expected outcome is a shared-looking plan for generating the case's 3D planning materials, assigning responsibilities between surgery and the 3D lab, and setting the delivery timeline.

members.name: Mr. David Okoro
members.expertise: Acetabular and pelvic fracture fixation, operative trauma planning, intraoperative reduction strategy
members.background: David is a senior surgeon at a regional major trauma centre who regularly manages complex pelvic and acetabular injuries and is trying to integrate 3D planning into selected trauma cases without slowing theatre scheduling.
members.private_state: He wants the case to proceed on time, wants enough 3D support to improve his reduction strategy, and hopes a smooth case will help justify wider adoption of 3D planning in the trauma service.
hidden_assumptions: If a CT series is already visible on PACS and good enough for diagnosis, it is usually good enough for practical 3D planning.
When surgeons ask for a '3D model,' the default is a clinically usable bone reconstruction for visual review and rough implant contouring, not an extensively engineered deliverable.
A 'planning pack' mainly means material for the consultant's own preoperative thinking and the Monday trauma conference, not a theatre-facing package.
If something needs to be 'ready by Monday,' that means available before the Monday morning fracture meeting starts.
Once the case is accepted by the 3D lab, any standard extras that are truly necessary will be handled automatically without needing explicit discussion.

members.name: Dr. Priya Nair
members.role: Lead 3D Imaging Scientist and Advanced Musculoskeletal Radiographer
members.expertise: CT post-processing, segmentation, printable STL generation, imaging protocol optimization for orthopaedic planning
members.background: Priya runs the hospital's small 3D planning service, supporting maxillofacial and orthopaedic teams, and is focused on producing technically defensible models from appropriate imaging data.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to succeed but is wary of producing inaccurate or low-value outputs from suboptimal scans, and she wants surgeons to see the service as rigorous rather than ad hoc image rendering.
hidden_assumptions: For trauma cases, 'the CT' relevant to 3D planning normally means a thin-slice in-house acquisition or a series that meets print-quality protocol, not just any diagnostic study on PACS.
A '3D model' for surgical planning normally includes cleaned segmentation, fragment separation where possible, contralateral mirroring, and export-ready files.
A 'planning pack' implies a standard set of outputs for downstream use by theatre staff as well as the surgeon, including printable files and templating views unless declined explicitly.
A deadline stated only as a day refers to completion by the end of that working day unless a meeting time is named.
If radiology protocol usually requires a repeat high-resolution scan, the surgical team already knows that and is planning around it.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the patient needs a '3D model' for planning.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a straightforward reconstructed hemipelvis he can inspect on screen and use mentally for reduction planning and rough plate contouring.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a validated segmentation package with separated fracture fragments, mirrored contralateral anatomy, and print-ready mesh files.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In orthopaedic discussion, '3D model' is an umbrella term used casually by both clinical and technical staff, so each assumes their own default level of detail is the obvious standard.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to producing the 'planning pack' for the case.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the planning pack is limited to material needed for his case review and Monday conference, such as screenshots or a digital reconstruction.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the planning pack includes broader downstream materials for theatre use, such as print files, templating views, and labelled outputs that support the operative team.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds routine and administrative, so neither person feels a need to itemize contents; each interprets it according to their service's normal workflow.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the materials should be 'ready by Monday'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means available before the 7:30 AM Monday pelvic trauma meeting so he can review it in that forum.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means completed and uploaded by close of business on Monday, still comfortably ahead of the scheduled operation later in the week.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Day-only deadlines are common in hospital coordination, and both are focused on the same surgical week, so the missing time boundary feels too ordinary to question.

misalignment_points.topic: Which scan 'the trauma CT' refers to
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about building the plan from 'the trauma CT' already associated with the case.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the outside-hospital CT from Saturday that has already been imported into PACS and reviewed clinically.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the expected in-house thin-slice pelvic CT series that should replace or supplement the outside scan for segmentation quality.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There is indeed a CT already in the record, and local workflows often silently upgrade imaging quality when needed, so each person believes they are referring to the same obvious study.

turns.inner_thought: This is exactly the sort of acetabular case where a basic 3D reconstruction would help me think through the reduction and whether I need to contour anything in advance. I do not want this turning into a big production that slows the list. If Priya can just take the CT that's already on PACS and get me a usable 3D model plus a planning pack before the Monday morning fracture meeting, that should be enough and would help show the service can support trauma in real time.
turns.utterance: Priya, I've got a complex acetabular fixation going up on Wednesday, and I'd really like 3D support for it. If we can have the 3D model and the planning pack ready by Monday, that would be ideal.

turns.inner_thought: Good, this sounds like a proper pilot case. If we're doing it properly, I can build from the trauma CT once the right pelvic acquisition is there, then produce the usual planning pack. For this kind of fracture, the mirrored side is often useful, and when surgeons ask for a 3D model I assume they want a defensible segmentation package, not just a quick rendering. Monday as a day target should be manageable.
turns.utterance: Yes, that should be possible. I can start from the trauma CT and put together the usual planning pack, and I can include the mirrored side as well if that would be helpful.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds fine. The main value for me is being able to rotate the hemipelvis, look at the fracture geometry, and talk through the reduction sequence with the team on Monday. I don't need an elaborate deliverable for this one; just something clinically clear enough to support my thinking and rough plate contouring.
turns.utterance: Yes, that would be useful. The main thing is that the model helps me talk through the reduction sequence at the fracture conference and get a sense of plate contouring beforehand.

turns.inner_thought: He's clearly thinking about operative planning, so I should proceed on the assumption of a full technical workflow. Once the pelvic series is in, I can do proper fragment work and finalize the mirrored reconstruction. I don't need to spell out the details now; this is standard for a planning request like this.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. Once the pelvic series is in, I can separate the major fragments and finalize the mirrored reconstruction for the planning outputs.

turns.inner_thought: Good, as long as I can see it before the 7:30 Monday trauma meeting. That's the real deadline, because the whole point is to shape the operative discussion there. I assume 'ready by Monday' already means that, but it doesn't hurt to mention the meeting.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'd like to review everything ahead of the Monday 7:30 trauma meeting so we can discuss the operative approach there.

turns.inner_thought: Monday should still be fine overall. The operation isn't until Wednesday, so if I complete and upload the pack during Monday that's well within a normal turnaround. I should also check whether they want a physical print, because for a standard planning pack I usually prepare for that unless told otherwise.
turns.utterance: Monday should work. Do you think theatre will want the print included, or is the digital planning pack sufficient?

turns.inner_thought: No need to add printing and complicate things. A digital reconstruction is enough for conference and for me to plan the case. I mainly want something practical in hand for review, not a full theatre package.
turns.utterance: Digital should be fine for now. The main thing is having something clear for conference review and my own pre-op planning.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine; they may not need the physical print, but I should still include the standard downstream files and templating views. Even if he only uses the digital material himself, the rest of the team often benefits later, and I want the service to look robust rather than ad hoc.
turns.utterance: No problem. I'll still export the printable files and the templating views as part of the standard pack, so the team has the full set if needed.

turns.inner_thought: The scan is already there, so hopefully she can just get on with it. If there is genuinely some technical issue with using the outside CT, she'll tell me, but otherwise I assume the standard necessities are handled automatically once the lab takes the case.
turns.utterance: Great. The trauma CT is already on PACS from the referring hospital, so just let me know if anything blocks segmentation.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, I'll keep an eye out for the pelvic CT coming through and then complete the full model on Monday. Once the proper series is available, I can finish the segmentation, generate the standard planning pack, and send it over when it's done. That should still be comfortably on time for a Wednesday case.
turns.utterance: Will do. I'll watch for the pelvic CT to come through, finalize the model Monday, and send the pack over once it's complete.
